items.locator: StatPearls Barrett Esophagus — Introduction/Etiology: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophagus; most cases are acquired and the usual precipitant is long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease, with increased esophageal adenocarcinoma risk.
items.version: StatPearls Barrett Esophagus updated 2025-05-26 and current in StatPearls [Internet] 2026; NCBI source live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with years of frequent gastroesophageal reflux asks about a long-term complication. Which condition is associated with chronic GERD?
items.rationale: Long-standing gastroesophageal reflux is the usual precipitating factor for acquired Barrett esophagus, making Option B correct. Achalasia is an esophageal motility disorder, esophageal varices are primarily related to portal hypertension, and Zenker diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal pouch rather than the characteristic metaplastic complication of chronic GERD.
items.finding: Fresh Rule 1 review removed explanatory padding from all four diagnostic choices and corrected difficulty from hard to easy because the item tests a direct chronic-GERD association. A second read confirmed a single supported answer and no diagnostic overlap in the options.

items.source_name: KDIGO — 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
items.locator: KDIGO 2024 CKD Guideline, Definition and classification of CKD, Kidney International 105(Suppl 4S), printed p. S137: CKD is classified based on Cause, GFR category (G1-G5), and Albuminuria category (A1-A3), abbreviated CGA; Tables 2 and 3 define the GFR and albuminuria categories.
items.version: KDIGO 2024 CKD Guideline remains the current global CKD guideline; focused Chapter 3 update is underway but has not superseded the classification section. PDF page S137 and currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A nurse explains chronic kidney disease classification to a client. Which framework reflects current KDIGO CKD classification?

options.A: Cause, blood-pressure category, and serum sodium category
options.B: Cause, GFR category, and albuminuria category
options.C: Cause, serum sodium category, and body-mass-index category
options.D: Cause, hemoglobin category, and blood-pressure category

items.rationale: KDIGO classifies CKD using the CGA framework: Cause, GFR category, and Albuminuria category, so Option B is correct. Blood pressure, serum sodium, body mass index, and hemoglobin may be clinically important but are not the three components of the KDIGO CKD classification framework.
items.finding: Fresh Rule 1 review directly rechecked the KDIGO primary PDF, including printed page S137, and removed rationale-like padding from the choices. The final options are parallel competing frameworks. Independent second-pass review found no alternate correct framework and preserved Reduction of Risk Potential because the item tests diagnostic classification.

items.locator: StatPearls Myxedema Coma — History and Physical/Evaluation: decompensated severe hypothyroidism typically features altered mental status and hypothermia, with bradycardia, hypotension or hypoventilation and multisystem dysfunction; it is a life-threatening endocrine emergency.
items.version: StatPearls Myxedema Coma updated 2025-12-13 and current in StatPearls [Internet] 2026; NCBI source live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with severe untreated hypothyroidism develops hypothermia, bradycardia, and a markedly decreased level of consciousness. Which complication is most likely?
items.rationale: Severe decompensated hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, and major alteration in mental status is characteristic of myxedema coma, so Option B is correct. Adrenal crisis and septic shock can cause hemodynamic instability but do not specifically match this severe hypothyroid pattern. Thyroid storm is severe thyrotoxicosis and typically produces the opposite hyperadrenergic pattern.
items.finding: Fresh Rule 1 review replaced padded, self-explanatory choices with concise clinically plausible endocrine/emergency diagnoses. Independent second-pass review confirmed that the severe hypothyroid context plus hypothermia, bradycardia, and depressed consciousness makes myxedema coma uniquely best.

items.source_name: Endocrine Society — Primary Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline
items.locator: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline — Primary Adrenal Insufficiency, clinical features and diagnostic considerations: glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency can cause fatigue or weakness, volume depletion and hypotension, salt craving, and hyperpigmentation from elevated ACTH in primary disease.
items.version: Endocrine Society Primary Adrenal Insufficiency guideline remains the current society guideline resource; live source and current status rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client has fatigue, hypotension, salt craving, and patchy hyperpigmentation. Which endocrine disorder best fits this pattern?
items.rationale: Primary adrenal insufficiency can produce fatigue or weakness, hypotension from volume depletion, salt craving from mineralocorticoid deficiency, and hyperpigmentation associated with elevated ACTH, so Option B is correct. Cushing syndrome reflects glucocorticoid excess, acromegaly reflects growth-hormone excess, and primary hyperaldosteronism typically produces hypertension rather than this pattern.
items.finding: Fresh Rule 1 review removed answer-explaining clauses from every choice. The concise endocrine diagnoses remain clinically plausible distractors without creating a second correct answer; the final item passed an independent second read against the Endocrine Society source.

items.locator: Mayo Clinic Laboratories Test KS/602352, Potassium, Serum — Reference Values: age >=1 year 3.6-5.2 mmol/L. Clinical Information/Interpretation: decreased extracellular potassium is characterized by muscle weakness and cardiac conduction abnormalities; potassium below 3.0 mmol/L is associated with marked neuromuscular symptoms.
items.version: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories Test KS/602352 catalog entry; reference interval and interpretation live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: An adult client has a serum potassium level of 2.9 mEq/L and reports new muscle weakness. Which interpretation is most accurate?
items.rationale: Mayo Clinic Laboratories lists the adult potassium reference interval as 3.6 to 5.2 mmol/L and notes that low extracellular potassium can produce muscle weakness; values below 3.0 mmol/L are associated with marked neuromuscular symptoms. A value of 2.9 mEq/L is therefore hypokalemia, making Option C correct. The other options either identify a different electrolyte abnormality or incorrectly classify the measured potassium as normal.
items.finding: Fresh Rule 1 audit corrected the source hierarchy from a general pathophysiology source to the required authoritative laboratory reference, Mayo Clinic Laboratories. It also removed padded explanatory choices and corrected difficulty from hard to easy because the value is directly below the cited adult reference interval. The corrected item passed a fresh second read for lab interpretation, cueing, and second-answer risk.

items.locator: Endotext/NCBI Bookshelf — Diabetic Ketoacidosis, Clinical Manifestations and diagnostic tables: DKA includes hyperglycemia, ketonemia/ketonuria, metabolic acidosis with pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L, and Kussmaul breathing described as deep, labored breathing.
items.version: Endotext Diabetic Ketoacidosis entry current in 2026; diagnostic criteria and clinical manifestations live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with poorly controlled diabetes has a serum glucose of 420 mg/dL, positive serum ketones, a bicarbonate level of 16 mEq/L, and rapid deep respirations. Which acid-base disturbance is most consistent with this presentation?
items.rationale: The combination of marked hyperglycemia, positive ketones, bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L, and deep Kussmaul-type respirations is consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis, whose primary acid-base disturbance is metabolic acidosis. Option D is correct. The rapid deep respirations represent respiratory compensation rather than a primary respiratory alkalosis, and neither metabolic alkalosis nor respiratory acidosis fits the ketotic low-bicarbonate presentation.
items.finding: Fresh Rule 1 audit identified a second-answer ambiguity in the prior version: low bicarbonate plus rapid deep breathing without ketone or hyperglycemia context could be misread as compensation for another primary disorder. The stem was clinically corrected by adding DKA-defining hyperglycemia and positive ketones, the choices were de-padded, and the final state was independently re-audited for a single best answer.

items.source_name: StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf — Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral Bone Disorder
items.locator: StatPearls Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral Bone Disorder — Pathophysiology: declining kidney function impairs phosphate excretion and calcitriol production, contributing to hyperphosphatemia, lower serum calcium or hypocalcemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism in advanced CKD.
items.version: Current StatPearls CKD-Mineral Bone Disorder entry in StatPearls [Internet] 2026; NCBI source live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with advanced chronic kidney disease has marked hyperphosphatemia. Which additional laboratory abnormality commonly accompanies this mineral-bone disturbance?
items.rationale: In advanced CKD, impaired phosphate excretion and reduced calcitriol activity contribute to phosphate retention and lower serum calcium, often with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Hypocalcemia is therefore the best answer. Hypercalcemia is the opposite calcium pattern, while hypernatremia and hypermagnesemia are not the characteristic paired abnormality tested in CKD mineral-bone disorder.
items.finding: Fresh Rule 1 review removed explanatory padding from the laboratory choices while preserving clinically distinct distractors. Independent second-pass review confirmed that hypocalcemia is the characteristic paired abnormality supported by the cited CKD-mineral bone pathophysiology and that no second option overlaps.

items.locator: StatPearls Neutrophilia — Etiology, Infection/Inflammation: infection and inflammation are common causes of reactive neutrophilia; bacterial infections are usually associated with a left shift, meaning increased band/immature neutrophil forms. The differential must be interpreted with the clinical presentation rather than treated as diagnostic alone.
items.version: StatPearls Neutrophilia, StatPearls [Internet] 2026; NCBI source live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.rationale: Neutrophilia can occur with infection and inflammation, and bacterial infections commonly produce a left shift with increased immature neutrophil forms. In a client with fever and productive cough, that pattern increases concern for an acute bacterial respiratory infection, but the CBC differential does not establish the diagnosis by itself. Option A appropriately integrates the laboratory pattern with the clinical presentation. Options B and C misstate the association, and Option D incorrectly ignores clinically relevant abnormalities.

items.locator: National Cancer Institute — Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) Test Fact Sheet: PSA is produced by normal and malignant prostate cells; levels can rise with prostate cancer but also with benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis/inflammation, and other factors, so an elevated PSA alone does not diagnose prostate cancer.
items.version: Current NCI PSA Fact Sheet live-rechecked 2026-08-15; difficulty corrected to easy because the item tests direct interpretation of a nonspecific tumor marker rather than multistep clinical judgment.

items.locator: National Cancer Institute — Ovarian Cancer Screening (PDQ), CA-125: CA-125 is associated with ovarian cancer but lacks diagnostic specificity; elevated values can occur in benign gynecologic/non-gynecologic conditions and other malignancies, so the result cannot diagnose ovarian cancer by itself.
items.version: Current NCI Ovarian Cancer Screening PDQ live-rechecked 2026-08-15; difficulty corrected to easy because the item tests direct nonspecific-marker interpretation.
